title: CNCF Score project improved its security posture by joining the Docker-Sponsored Open Source Program
summary: See how CNCF Score improved container security with Docker Scout, Hardened Images, and the Docker-Sponsored Open Source Program.
body_markdown:
Score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the[Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program](https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/repos/manage/trusted-content/dsos-program/) to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default.


## The Opportunity


In September 2025,[the CNCF announced a partnership with Docker](https://www.cncf.io/announcements/2025/09/18/cncf-expands-infrastructure-support-for-project-maintainers-through-partnership-with-docker/) to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost.


This aligned closely with the discussions held at the[Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta](https://contribute.cncf.io/blog/2025/11/08/maintainer-summit-update-from-the-project-staff) , which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.


The[Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program](https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/repos/manage/trusted-content/dsos-program/) supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure.


Eligible projects receive:


- Verified Docker-Sponsored Open Source badge
- Removal of rate limits for developers
- Access to Docker Scout for software supply chain management
- Insights and analytics
- Repository logo
- Improved discoverability on Docker Hub


## Docker Hub


**Before:** Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of[score-compose](https://github.com/score-spec/score-compose) ,[score-k8s](https://github.com/score-spec/score-k8s) ,[score-helm](https://github.com/score-spec/score-helm) and[score-radius](https://github.com/score-spec/score-radius) ; and the[sample-score-app](https://github.com/score-spec/sample-score-app) used for demos and testing. We previously published them in the GitHub Container Registry[here](https://github.com/orgs/score-spec/packages) .


**After:** Through the DSOS Program, we now publish these images on Docker Hub, which increases their visibility and gives the community a verified, trusted source.


All the container images are now available[on Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/u/scorespec) .

## Docker Scout


**Before:** As a CNCF project, Score follows the[OpenSSF best practices](https://www.bestpractices.dev/en) . In addition, the[OpenSSF Scorecard GitHub Action](https://securityscorecards.dev/) runs continuously. This was a solid foundation, but we had no dedicated security scanning tool in place.


**After:** The DSOS Program gave us access to Docker Scout, which we now use in our pull requests and on our container registry (Docker Hub). This gives us clear visibility into the CVEs introduced or fixed by each pull request and release.


The following GitHub Actions step uses` docker/scout-action` on every pull request to compare the image built from the PR branch with the one built from the main branch:


```text
- name: Docker Scout Comparison between main branch and current PR branch
uses: docker/scout-action@v1
with:
command: compare
image: local://score-compose:pr-${{ github.event.number }}
to: local://score-compose:main
write-comment: true
github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
organization: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}


```


Here is an example of a comment posted by this` docker/scout-action` step in a recent Pull Request:


The comment details the comparison between the two images (before versus after): size, packages updated, added or removed, CVEs introduced and resolved, and compliance with our[policies in place](https://docs.docker.com/scout/policy/) (run as non-root, no critical CVEs, no packages with AGPL v3 licences).


The analysis goes beyond the images themselves: it also covers the Go libraries and binaries they contain.


The Docker Scout console also provides a single view of CVEs, packages, base images, and policies across all of our container images, which makes it easy to see what is used where, and in which version.


## Docker Hardened Images


When[Docker made Hardened Images freely available under Apache 2.0](https://www.docker.com/press-release/docker-makes-hardened-images-free-open-and-transparent-for-everyone/) , we saw an opportunity to simplify our security posture while staying compatible with our existing Dockerfiles and workflows, even though we were already using multi-stage builds and distroless base images.


Docker Hardened Images are minimal, security-focused container base images designed to reduce inherited risk in downstream projects. They are built and maintained with security and transparency as defaults, and offer:


- Minimal attack surface: Only required components are included.
- Non-root execution: Images run as non-root by default.
- Supply chain security: Includes published SBOMs and SLSA Level 3 build provenance.
- Active maintenance: Images are patched and rebuilt as vulnerabilities are disclosed.
- Open standards: All images are reproducible, open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0, making them compatible with CNCF governance and distribution models.


The migration was straightforward.


Take the score-radius CLI, which used a golang:alpine and a distroless images and now uses[dhi.io/golang](https://dhi.io/catalog/golang) and[dhi.io/static](https://dhi.io/catalog/static) images. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:


In the associated PR[here](https://github.com/score-spec/sample-score-app/pull/58) , image size dropped by 0.3 MB while the number of packages stayed the same and the CVE count remained at 0. We could have stayed with Debian, but chose to move to an Alpine base image (DHI provides the[two options](https://docs.docker.com/dhi/core-concepts/glibc-musl/) ):


The same applies to the NodeJS sample-score-app, which used nodejs on top of an alpine image and now uses a[dhi.io/node](https://dhi.io/catalog/node) image. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:


In the associated PR[here](https://github.com/score-spec/score-radius/pull/28) , 22 packages were removed (including the package manager and the shell), along with 2 CVEs:

## Docker GitHub Builder


Although not directly part of the DSOS Program, we took the opportunity to adopt the new[docker/github-builder GitHub reusable workflow](https://docs.docker.com/build/ci/github-actions/github-builder/architecture/) to release our container images.


This model provides a build pipeline maintained in the Docker organization, with a version-controlled BuildKit environment, multi-platform builds distributed across runners where beneficial, and signed SLSA provenance recording both the source commit and the builder identity.


The trade-off is intentional. You retain control over when the build runs and which inputs it uses, while the build implementation itself lives in the Docker-maintained workflow rather than in per-repository job steps.


**Before** , the GitHub Actions workflow to release our container images was using this sequence of actions:


- ` docker/setup-buildx-action`
- ` docker/login-action`
- ` docker/build-push-action`
- ` cosign sign`


```text
release-container-image:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
permissions:
id-token: write
packages: write
steps:
- name: Set up Docker Buildx
uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
- name: Login to Docker Hub (docker.io)
uses: docker/login-action@v4
with:
registry: docker.io
username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}
password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_RELEASE_TOKEN }}
- name: Login to GitHub Container Registry
uses: docker/login-action@v4
with:
registry: ghcr.io
username: ${{ github.actor }}
password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
- name: Build and push docker image
id: build-push-container
uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
with:
context: .
platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
push: true
provenance: mode=max
sbom: true
tags: |
ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose:${{ github.ref_name }}
ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose:latest
docker.io/scorespec/score-compose:${{ github.ref_name }}
docker.io/scorespec/score-compose:latest
build-args: |
"VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}"
- name: Sign container image
run: |
cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose@${{ steps.build-push-container.outputs.digest }}
cosign sign --yes scorespec/score-compose@${{ steps.build-push-container.outputs.digest }}


```


**After** , this same workflow is now only using the reusable workflow` docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml` :


```text
release-container-image:
uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1
permissions:
contents: read
id-token: write
packages: write
with:
output: image
push: true
platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
sbom: true
cache: true
context: .
set-meta-labels: true
set-meta-annotations: true
build-args: |
"VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}"
meta-images: |
ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose
scorespec/score-compose
meta-tags: |
type=ref,event=tag
latest
registry-identities: |
- type: dockerhub
registry: docker.io
username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}
connection_id: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }}
secrets:
registry-auths: |
- registry: ghcr.io
username: ${{ github.actor }}
password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}


```


Docker GitHub Builder gives us a Docker-maintained build pipeline with signed SLSA provenance and SBOM attestations, helping consumers verify the builder identity and trace images back to their source commit. Signing uses GitHub OIDC, so we don’t need to manage long-lived signing keys. With caching enabled in our workflow, cache entries are also signed and verified before reuse, helping protect against cache poisoning. See the[Docker GitHub Builder documentation](https://docs.docker.com/build/ci/github-actions/github-builder/) for more information about its security model.


The following command verifies the signature on the attestation manifest for the selected image platform:


```text
TAG=latest
PLATFORM=amd64


SIGNED_DIGEST=$(crane manifest scorespec/score-compose:$TAG \
| jq -r --arg platformdigest \
"$(crane digest --platform linux/$PLATFORM scorespec/score-compose:$TAG)" \
'.manifests[] | select(.annotations["vnd.docker.reference.digest"] == $platformdigest) | .digest')


cosign verify \
--experimental-oci11 \
--new-bundle-format \
--certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
--certificate-identity-regexp  '^https://github\.com/docker/github-builder/\.github/workflows/build\.yml@.*$' \
scorespec/score-compose@$SIGNED_DIGEST


```


## OIDC Connections


Most recently, with an update released on July 21, 2026, Docker introduced[OIDC connections](https://docs.docker.com/security/authentication/oidc-connections/) . This feature allows pulls and pushes to Docker Hub to use a short-lived token instead of a long-lived Organization Access Token (OAT).


An OIDC connection establishes a trust relationship between Docker and a trusted third party, so you no longer need to maintain long-lived credentials. Docker exchanges short-lived tokens with the other vendor, which can grant fine-grained access to your Docker resources.


**Before:**


With` docker/login-action` :


```text
steps:
- uses: docker/login-action@v4
with:
username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}
password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN }}


```


Or with` docker/github-builder` :


```text
uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1
with:
...
secrets:
registry-auths: |
- username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}
password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN }}


```


**After:**


With` docker/login-action` :


```text
permissions:
id-token: write
steps:
- uses: docker/login-action@v4 # v4.5.0+
env:
DOCKERHUB_OIDC_CONNECTIONID: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }}
with:
username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}


```


Or with` docker/github-builder` :


```text
uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 # v1.15.0+
permissions:
id-token: write
with:
...
registry-identities: |
- type: dockerhub
registry: docker.io
username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }}
connection_id: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }}


```


By replacing a static, long-lived token with a short-lived one and making it issued on a per-workflow basis, we removed a credential that could otherwise be stolen and misused.


## Wrapping Up


Participating in the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program has been rewarding, and it has helped Score adopt a security-by-default foundation. Using[Docker Scout](https://docs.docker.com/scout/) ,[Docker Hardened Images](https://docs.docker.com/dhi/) ,[OIDC connections](https://docs.docker.com/enterprise/security/oidc-connections/) , and the[Docker GitHub Builder](https://docs.docker.com/build/ci/github-actions/github-builder/) has strengthened the security posture of our container images and brought broader benefits to the Score projects and repositories.


If you maintain a CNCF project or any open source project, we encourage you to explore the[Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program](https://www.docker.com/community/open-source/application/) . The security improvements were measurable, and the onboarding process was straightforward.


The full implementation across the Score repositories is tracked in[GitHub issue #376](https://github.com/score-spec/score-compose/issues/376) .

Feel free to connect with the Score maintainers during the Maintainer Summit on Sunday, Nov 8th and at the Kiosk #P-17B on Thursday, Nov 12th between 10:15am and 2pm, you will see[Score in actions with the new Score Labspace](https://score.dev/blog/score-labspace/) !


*Note: This work was completed after I joined Docker. It was, however, an initiative we wanted to pursue as CNCF project maintainers from the moment it was*[announced in September 2025](https://www.cncf.io/announcements/2025/09/18/cncf-expands-infrastructure-support-for-project-maintainers-through-partnership-with-docker/) *, both to improve our security posture and to share what we learned with the broader community.*


We hope this post helps you strengthen the security of your own projects.
